For a few weeks in 1987, trash was temporarily headline news: a barge filled with waste that would no longer fit in New York City’s overflowing landfills spent months wandering up and down the East Coast with nowhere to dump its smelly, rotting cargo. The trash barge’s travels triggered a long overdue public rethink of the wisdom of sending all of our waste to landfills—including food. But fast forward more than thirty years, and food still takes up more space in American landfills than anything else. About 30 to 40 percent of food produced in the US gets thrown away, rather than eaten. What’s more, putting all that rotting food inside landfills produces a lot of methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. Our ancestors knew exactly what to do with food waste; the earliest descriptions of composting were written on clay tablets more than 4,000 years ago. So why didn’t the GarBarge kick off a composting craze? And why is it so hard for us to keep food waste out of landfills? This episode, Gastropod visits the future of food waste: the high-tech facilities as well as the innovative policies that promise to keep our discarded food out of landfills, keep methane from escaping into the atmosphere, and turn those food scraps into something useful. Can a state the size of California really keep 75 percent of its food waste out of landfills, as it has pledged to do by 2025—and what will happen if it does? Listen in for compost blow-dryers, fruit-sticker bingo, and a lot of microbes! Superfund sites are some of the most polluted areas in the country, containing highly toxic waste such as asbestos, lead, and dioxin. Cleaning them up, which follows a systematic, science-based process as required by law, can take decades.There are more than 1,300 of these sites across the US, from Florida’s Panhandle to the banks of the Rio Grande in New Mexico. They’re found in nearly every state, often near residential areas. The EPA estimates that 78 million people live within three miles of a Superfund site—nearly 1 in 4 Americans.But these waste dumps face a growing threat: the worsening effects of climate change. The EPA has determined that more than 300 Superfund sites are at risk of flooding. The actual number of flood-prone sites, however, may be more than twice that amount, according to a 2021 Government Accountability Office report. Extreme Heat Is the New Normal
New York Times Opinion, 08 28, 2026

Video (15:42)




Description
We filmed “A New Inferno,” the short documentary above, in Phoenix, one of the hottest cities in America, through some of the city’s hottest days of 2025, during one of the hottest years on record globally. On one of our production days, temperatures reached 118 while we were filming outside.
In the face of extreme heat, we documented firefighters and paramedics of the Phoenix Fire Department saving lives in real time. We wanted to call attention to a specialized technique of ice bag immersion for people facing life-threatening heat stroke. We hope that telling their story and showcasing the efficacy of this strategy will encourage wider adoption of this protocol across the country.
Yet this procedure is ultimately a stopgap, as firefighters do their best to adapt to the climate crisis in front of them. The underlying story of heat in Phoenix is one of broader, interlocking crises: homelessness and substance use disorders that are deeply entangled with urban heat, each amplifying the other, illustrating how climate change affects the disenfranchised most brutally.
With our film, we aim to reframe how the public thinks about heat: as an invisible, silent killer reshaping the rhythms of urban life.

0:04 · Cooling, whether that’s air conditioning or refrigerators is probably one of the biggest challenges we face with respect to climate change.

0:24 · Global demand for air conditioning is predicted to triple by 2050.


0:29 · Meeting that demand is a challenge that’s at the heart of both the climate and cost of living crises around the world.


0:36 · I think the problem is very rancid because we see the prices of electricity going up.

###### Cool roofs


1:10 · Dr. Denia Kolokotsa has been studying energy efficiency in buildings for the last three decades.


1:17 · When I started doing this research everybody said that I was crazy.


1:21 · You know, what are you going to do?


1:23 · Now, I think everybody speaks about that.


1:26 · So that’s the difference.


1:29 · Denia has studied a deceptively simple solution to our cooling problem.


1:34 · Cool roofs.


1:35 · Mainly that can be tiles, paints, shingles whatever it is attached within a roof that has the ability to reflect the sunlight and emit the thermal energy that is absorbed by the surfaces.


1:52 · If it sounds a bit low tech to you that’s probably the point.


1:55 · This simple, yet effective solution has been around for centuries.


1:59 · It’s rooted in the concept of passive cooling used in ancient architecture.


2:05 · For example, passive cooling in Cyclades in Greece is to paint the buildings white to emit the sun back to the sky.


2:16 · Passive cooling in Egypt is to have smaller openings and smaller windows in order not to allow the sun to come in.

2:27 · Madrid is notoriously hot in the summer.

2:34 · It has the mammoth task of keeping thousands of workers and fish cool under its massive roof.

3:25 · With thousands of people and fish sloshing in and out, keeping everything cold is a top priority.


3:33 · In 2018, the market underwent a 3 million Euro makeover to do just that.


3:51 · The entire roof was cleaned and repainted with a waterproof and highly reflective coating.


4:08 · The project also added 68 evaporative cooling units to supply a constant stream of cold air into the market.


4:33 · Mercamadrid says the new system saves up to 70% energy and cuts 34 tons of carbon emissions a year.

#### How America’s hottest city is trying to cool down

##### Description


Can trees help save Phoenix from extreme heat?


Subscribe and turn on notifications 🔔 so you don’t miss any videos: http://goo.gl/0bsAjO


It’s time to stop looking at trees as a form of “beautification.” They are, instead, a living form of infrastructure, providing a variety of services that include stormwater management, air filtering, carbon sequestration, and, most importantly for a city like Phoenix, Arizona, they cool the environment around them.


Trees can lower neighborhood temperatures in three ways: 1) Their shade prevents solar radiation from hitting paved surfaces like concrete and asphalt, which absorb energy and rerelease it into the air as heat. 2) Their leaves pull heat from the immediate area in order to evapotranspirate water that’s drawn from the soil. And, 3) If you’re standing under one, a tree protects your body directly from the sun’s rays. If you’ve ever made a summer visit to a dry, hot city like Phoenix, you’ll know how important shade is for making any outdoor experiences tolerable.


As Phoenix deals with a rising frequency of extreme heat waves — which aren’t only deadly, but also cause worrisome spikes in energy demand — the city is looking to trees as part of its heat mitigation strategy. Phoenix isn’t devoid of trees, but they’re distributed unevenly across the city. A quick glance at a satellite image of the metro area reveals substantial green splotches in the north and east and brown ones in the south and west, where many lower-income neighborhoods are located.


So Phoenix recently pledged to reach “tree equity” by 2030, under an agreement with American Forests, a national tree organization. I visited Phoenix recently to take a look at the current state of the city’s urban forest. In this video, we use drone imagery and thermal cameras to understand how the urban design of the city contributes to extreme heat, and what it can do to cool down.

Heat is the deadliest weather hazard in the U.S. and many places around the world, and it’s only getting worse.

Paige Bierma, 02-21-2021

Documentary Film (26:48)




Description
In Waking Up to Wildfires, Emmy-winning filmmaker Paige Bierma uses her camera to tell the stories of people most affected by the 2017 North Bay wildfires. We hear from survivors, firefighters, public health officials, community groups and scientists trying to make sense of it all while people struggle to recover and new fires erupt.
The UC Davis Environmental Health Sciences Center produced Waking Up to Wildfires with a grant from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences to help shed light on the plight communities face after these types of disasters.
You’re watching a condensed version (26 minutes long) that’s currently airing on PBS stations across the country. To find out more or get a copy, visit our website at environmentalhealth.ucdavis.edu.

title: Drought
text:
What we lose if the Great Salt Lake dries up


Duration: 00:12:31
Released: 2023
Series: Short Wave



Open Episode in Spotify
Open Series in Spotify
Dotted across the Great Basin of the American West are salty, smelly lakes. The largest of these, by far, is the Great Salt Lake in Utah.But a recent report found that water diversions for farming, climate change and population growth could mean the lake essentially disappears within five years. Less water going in means higher concentrations of salt and minerals, which threatens the crucial ecological role saline lakes play across the West, as well as the health of the people who live nearby. On today’s episode, Kirk takes Short Wave co-host Aaron Scott on an audio field trip to the endangered Great Salt Lake, and explains why losing the lake could be devastating for everyone from brine flies to the humans that live next door. See pcm.adswizz.com for information about our collection and use of personal data for sponsorship and to manage your podcast sponsorship preferences.NPR Privacy Policy



EMILY KWONG, BYLINE: You’re listening to SHORT WAVE from NPR.
AARON SCOTT, HOST:
Hey, SHORT WAVErs. Time to slip on those rubber boots because we’re off for a field trip with NPR correspondent Kirk Siegler. Hey, Kirk.
KIRK SIEGLER, BYLINE: Hey, Aaron.
SCOTT: So where are you taking us today?
SIEGLER: Well, we’re going to the Great Salt Lake in Utah. I trekked out there earlier this winter with Carly Biedul. She’s a biologist with the Great Salt Lake Institute.
CARLY BIEDUL: These might even be my footprints from last week.
SIEGLER: Carly is bundled up in an orange, puffy jacket, gloves and hat. And most importantly, she’s wearing thick, sturdy, rubber boots ’cause the mud with the frozen slick layer of ice on top is treacherous.
BIEDUL: Probably not fully, fully fresh, but…
SIEGLER: But the only thing we’re not prepared for is the stench.
This is pungent right here.
BIEDUL: Yeah.
SIEGLER: Smells like dead fish, almost.
SCOTT: Oh, yes. I’ve been on similar salty lakes here in Oregon. Whew. That smell is intense and immense.
SIEGLER: It is. And the stink is actually a good thing because it’s a sign of a biologically healthy saline lake.
BIEDUL: People have been saying that they miss the lake stink ’cause it just makes it feel like home, and it’s just not here anymore. So you’re lucky that it gets to smell so bad.
SCOTT: Oh, so the smell is disappearing?
SIEGLER: It is. Because, Aaron, the Great Salt Lake is drying and dying. Biedul hikes out here weekly. She’s trying to collect samples of tiny brine fly larva, which are getting harder and harder to find.
BIEDUL: I’m going to get my jar out.
SIEGLER: So think of it, the brine flies she’s looking for are at the bottom of the food chain. They’re feed for the migrating birds and so on. And most of the water that’s left out there is too salty now.
BIEDUL: The threshold is - we’re kind of at the threshold. So if things get any saltier, we’re super, super worried.
SIEGLER: And they may have good reason. A recent report says climate change, farming and population growth in Utah may dry up the lake in five years.
SCOTT: So today on the show - the future of the Great Salt Lake and similar lakes across the West. Why are they drying up? And what’ll we lose if they do? I’m Aaron Scott, and you’re listening to SHORT WAVE, the daily science podcast from NPR.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
SCOTT: OK, Kirk. So to begin, I’d love it if you would just paint us a picture of the Great Salt Lake, for those who’ve never had the pleasure of seeing it. What does it look like, and how did a big, salty lake end up so far from the ocean?
SIEGLER: Well, it - I can’t even overstate how large it is. It’s huge. And especially in the winter, it’s quite eerie. When we were out there, it was foggy and otherworldly and very, very shallow. In fact, we - you know, you heard there, trekking out in the mud where there should have been water because the lake is receding. So to answer your question, these saline lakes occur at the bottom of basins where there’s no way for the water to flow out to the sea. So basically, in Utah, when all the snow off the Wasatch Mountains right by Salt Lake City melts, it pools into the rivers, into these lakes in the spring and then they evaporate over the summer, leaving all sorts of particles behind and minerals, including saline.
SCOTT: And as you said, I mean, these saline lakes occur all across the Great Basin in the West. And they - they’re actually essential ecosystems, right?
SIEGLER: Exactly. They’re very important for migrating birds at the top of the food chain. And so when Carly Biedul is out there looking for larva at the bottom of the food chain, that’s an indicator of a potential ecological collapse. And I’m not being dramatic. These lakes occur in the Great Basin from Utah to Nevada, across to eastern California, even in parts of Oregon, as you say. There’s this huge geological anomaly. And a lot of these lakes have dried up over time. Some naturally, but a lot due to water diversions. Utah’s Wasatch Front, where the majority of the state’s population lives along Salt Lake City, is one of the fastest-growing places in the country. So water is in high demand. But also, just like across the West, most of the water being diverted out of the rivers that would be going to the Great Salt Lake are being diverted for farming and, in particular in Northern Utah, alfalfa farming in the high desert.
SCOTT: So water diversions is playing a huge role in why they’re disappearing. I’m guessing climate change also plays a role?
SIEGLER: Yes, because we’re in the West and - I don’t have to tell you - we’re in the midst of a 23-year megadrought. So drought and climate change are a big factor.
SCOTT: And so if these lakes are essential stopovers for birds as they migrate from Alaska and Canada down to South America, I mean, just millions of birds kind of stopping here, like this rest stop all-you-can-eat buffet, what’s it going to mean for them if these lakes dry up?
SIEGLER: Well, it’s another species that we know will be in peril. This is an essential flyover spot for migratory birds, and the effects could be devastating.
SCOTT: And it’s not just the birds, of course. I mean, there’s a lot of creatures around the lakes that depend on them, including us humans. What’s it going to mean for us?
SIEGLER: Well, one of the most immediate impacts may be pollution. This is a dried-up lake bed. And we’ve seen this in other parts of the West. Dust storms off of a dried-up lake bed that has toxins in it - naturally occurring toxins - blowing into a large population base will have untold impacts on health. And the Salt Lake City area, particularly in the winter, already has some of the dirtiest air in the nation as a result of natural inversions that occur in that basin, but also a lot of cars and a lot of other industries. So that’s the most immediate impact. But then there are also trickle-down effects, as well. There’s tourism. There’s mining that depends on the lake, and Utah’s famous ski resorts actually benefit from getting more snow from lake effect storms. So the impacts are countless, to be honest.
SCOTT: I mean, given all of that, Kirk, I’m guessing there’s probably a lot of outcry and activism and such going on by people living near the lake, right?
SIEGLER: There is. This is a huge topic that’s all over the news these days.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED NEWS ANCHOR #1: Utah still remains in a drought.
UNIDENTIFIED NEWS ANCHOR #2: Now to what some tonight are calling a looming environmental nuclear bomb in Utah. The mighty Great Salt Lake is drying up and…
UNIDENTIFIED NEWS ANCHOR #3: As the Great Salt Lake continues to shrink, a…
SIEGLER: Some of the neighborhoods that are closest to the lake, it’s a huge concern. I met Turner Bitton. He’s a community activist and neighborhood council leader in Salt Lake City’s West Valley.
TURNER BITTON: If the lake bed dries up and we’re having winds blowing dust storms into our neighborhood, the heavy metals are going to land right on top of this neighborhood.
SCOTT: Nobody wants giant clouds of toxic dust blanketing their backyard.
SIEGLER: They don’t. And he’s particularly concerned there because these neighborhoods in the West Valley - they’re more working class. They’re already hemmed in by two busy freeways. There’s a planned freeway expansion. Salt Lake City International Airport is right there and Utah’s largest oil refinery.
BITTON: I mean, we’re talking about something that could potentially make these neighborhoods - I don’t want to say uninhabitable - but for those that are vulnerable, for those that have lung issues, uninhabitable.
SCOTT: Is he being a little dramatic there, Kirk?
SIEGLER: He really isn’t. You know, researchers have found higher rates of asthma and cardiovascular disease in neighborhoods like these. And one University of Utah study even showed that students in schools around there scored lower on tests during bad air days. Dr. Brian Moench is president of Utah Physicians for a Healthy Environment. He says the state should have declared an emergency years ago.
BRIAN MOENCH: A lot of people think that dust is pretty benign because it’s, quote, \“natural.\” Well, that’s not the case. And in the case of dust from the Great Salt Lake, it is particularly toxic because we know that it’s laced with high concentrations of heavy metals.
SIEGLER: And most of Utah’s 3 million or so residents live just east of the lake along the Wasatch Mountains. Now, the lake is about 9 feet lower than normal right now, despite a good winter. And locals are already complaining of these dust storms.
SCOTT: OK, Kirk, so a lot of people upset about this. What’s being done about it? Is there any sort of movement in, like, the state legislature?
SIEGLER: There is. And there are a lot of promises so far, but it’s been remarkable in this, you know, politically divided time in a Republican-controlled state, how - in particular, how there’s bipartisan agreement over trying to fix the lake. There was a lot of pressure on lawmakers to do that. Some ideas floated, I have to say, sounded a bit like sci-fi - cloud seeding, even a pipeline to pump Pacific Ocean water in. Not exactly the same thing…
SCOTT: Wow.
SIEGLER: …But everything seems to be on the table. Lawmakers this past session debated setting a target elevation for the lake and also a half-billion-dollar package that would do things like pay farmers and cities to use less water. Here’s Republican Governor Spencer Cox in his recent State of the State address.
(SOUNDBITE OF SPEECH)
SPENCER COX: Earlier this month, a report predicted that in just five short years, the Great Salt Lake will completely disappear. Let me be absolutely clear - we are not going to let that happen.
SCOTT: Wow. Strong words. So did they pass any of those measures?
SIEGLER: Sort of? You know, they didn’t pass any big water use regulations or major targets for the lake. Now, they did include money in the budget for more water conservation, but they took out language from a bill that would have required the conserved water actually make it to the lake. The federal government, though, is also a player here, and they’re clearly paying attention. In the final days of last year, you had President Biden signing a bipartisan bill called the Saline Lake Ecosystems in the Great Basin States Program Act. Yeah.
SCOTT: That is a mouthful.
SIEGLER: Right. Well, but what you need to know - it allocates $25 million for the U.S. Geological Survey to work with other agencies - local land managers, scientists and nonprofits - to study and monitor these saline lakes in the Great Basin and come up with a conservation plan. But, you know, there’s a real sense of urgency here with the Great Salt Lake if, in fact, it could dry up in five years.
SCOTT: So the idea is we need more information before we can come up with a plan.
SIEGLER: Yeah. But, you know, in large part, I think it’s going to come down to the states because they manage the water rights. Last year, the Utah legislature did approve some money to try to buy up water rights. But pointing to the Salt Lake Tribune, they’ve been reporting that no farmers have actually taken them up on it. And this is a thing across the West right now, although we did get news just this week that one powerful player in Utah who you might have heard of - The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints - they’re getting involved. They’ve announced that they will permanently donate 20,000 acre feet of their water rights to the lake. So it’s something.
SCOTT: I think I hear those little brine fly larvae rejoicing just a little bit.
SIEGLER: You can. Wow. That’s good. So we don’t have to end on such a doom and gloom note. And I have to tell you, down at the lake, trekking out there with Carly Biedul, the biologist - she’s privy to all these negative headlines, and she goes out there every week. But she is just trying to stay positive herself.
BIEDUL: And that’s kind of what we’ve been trying to do - is find these moments to see the beauty when it’s so sad.
SIEGLER: It is beautiful out there. But Biedul says it’s sad because there’s not much time left to save the Great Salt Lake.
SCOTT: Thank you, as always, for bringing this to us, Kirk.
SIEGLER: You’re welcome.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
SCOTT: This episode was produced by Margaret Cirino and Liz Metzger, edited by Gabriel Spitzer and fact-checked by Anil Oza. Our audio engineer was Jay Czys. Brendan Crump is our podcast coordinator. Beth Donovan is the senior director of programming. And Anya Grundmann is the senior vice president of programming. I’m Aaron Scott. Thanks for listening to SHORT WAVE from NPR.

SIEGLER: They don’t. And he’s particularly concerned there because these neighborhoods in the West Valley - they’re more working class. They’re already hemmed in by two busy freeways. There’s a planned freeway expansion. Salt Lake City International Airport is right there and Utah’s largest oil refinery.
BITTON: I mean, we’re talking about something that could potentially make these neighborhoods - I don’t want to say uninhabitable - but for those that are vulnerable, for those that have lung issues, uninhabitable.

SIEGLER: He really isn’t. You know, researchers have found higher rates of asthma and cardiovascular disease in neighborhoods like these. SCOTT: Thank you, as always, for bringing this to us, Kirk.
SIEGLER: You’re welcome.

Dotted across the Great Basin of the American West are salty, smelly lakes. The largest of these, by far, is the Great Salt Lake in Utah.But a recent report found that water diversions for farming, climate change and population growth could mean the lake essentially disappears within five years. Less water going in means higher concentrations of salt and minerals, which threatens the crucial ecological role saline lakes play across the West, as well as the health of the people who live nearby. On today’s episode, Kirk takes Short Wave co-host Aaron Scott on an audio field trip to the endangered Great Salt Lake, and explains why losing the lake could be devastating for everyone from brine flies to the humans that live next door. SCOTT: And it’s not just the birds, of course. I mean, there’s a lot of creatures around the lakes that depend on them, including us humans. What’s it going to mean for us?

There’s mining that depends on the lake, and Utah’s famous ski resorts actually benefit from getting more snow from lake effect storms. So the impacts are countless, to be honest.

SIEGLER: There is. This is a huge topic that’s all over the news these days.

The Colorado River is running out — and the Imperial Valley is ground zero. As policymakers battle over rights to a shrinking river, farmers are grappling with the practical realities of growing food with less water. The Imperial Valley oasis
0:01 · The Imperial Valley sits downstream of two massive reservoirs: Lake Powell and Lake Mead.
0:08 · Together, they act as a giant savings account, buffering water users from the whims of weather and the uncertainty of the annual snowpack.
0:18 · The incongruous, almost magical, nature of this lush oasis in the desert really dawned on me during a visit to Gina Dockstader’s Citrus Grove.
0:29 · DOCKSTADER: What do you think, Lalo, you want to pick one off for us?
0:32 · This one right here? DOCKSTADER: Yeah.

1:21 · Right.
1:22 · High economic value in a small area.

1:31 · I am fourth-generation, and my son is fifth-generation.
1:34 · We are very, very proud of that fact.

2:02 · You can’t put all your eggs in one basket, right?

2:05 · O’BRIEN: No crop demands more Colorado River water than alfalfa.

2:49 · I will say…

3:21 · But Gina says folks in the Imperial Valley are accustomed to being in the crosshairs.
3:27 · DOCKSTADER: We’ve always felt that other people were looking at our water because we have such a significant… priority right.
3:34 · You think municipalities are gonna come in, you think the cities are gonna come and, and take our water.


Water management and policy
3:40 · O’BRIEN: That’s exactly what happened in 2003.
3:43 · As it became clear the Colorado River could no longer meet all the demands placed on it, the federal government required California to live within its legal allocation.
3:55 · The result was the Quantification Settlement Agreement, or QSA.
4:00 · It requires the Imperial Irrigation District to transfer water to San Diego.
4:06 · In return, the San Diego County Water Authority helps fund conservation projects that enable farmers to use less water while keeping much of their land in production.
4:18 · DOCKSTADER: Now I can pay for a sprinkler pipe.

4:28 · Farmers are resilient.

4:52 · I got 9.3…
4:55 · feet going into the field.

Adapting to a limited supply
7:04 · Farmers are paid to cease irrigating some of their crops during the hot summer months when evaporation is at its peak.

8:04 · But everything has its limits.
8:08 · It’s hard to do this with less water is what it comes down to. - Exactly, yeah, and we’re all on a budget. We’re all on a water budget.
8:15 · We have an apportionment…
8:19 · So, we have an apportionment and we have to live within that apportionment, and…
8:25 · that’s it, you know, so we have to be careful with our water.

Description
In Singapore, water supply impacted wars, the economy and people’s health. Now, one of the most water-stressed countries is teaching the world how to handle water when there is hardly any. 
#PlanetA #Singapore #WaterCrisis

Chapters:
00:00 Intro
00:35 The challenge
01:56 History

07:18 Step 4: NEWater
09:22 Policy and Education
10:14 Conclusion


Transcript

Intro
0:01 · No joke, but this place…
0:02 · has a serious issue with water.
0:06 · Water here has changed the course of war, started fights with neighboring countries, and dominates the city’s political agenda.
0:14 · And yet, this country is a role model.
0:18 · “Singapore got it right, as simple as that.”
0:20 · This is how Singapore is transforming itself from one of the most water-stressed countries in the world to self-sufficiency, from water rags – to riches.


The challenge
0:36 · Welcome to Singapore!
0:37 · A vibrant multicultural city-state, right on the equator.
0:41 · Densely populated, around 6 million people live on this tiny island.
0:45 · It’s an international hub for trade and finance.
0:48 · It’s clean, safe, modern, wealthy, green.
0:52 · Basically, it has a lot of everything you’d want.
0:55 · There’s just that one thing…
0:56 · Singapore has no natural freshwater resources.
1:00 · And the way its economy and population are growing, total water demand could almost double by 2060.
1:06 · But Singapore is on it.
1:10 · “None of what they’ve done is magic.”
1:13 · That’s Peter Gleick, he’s an award-winning water expert.
1:16 · He puts Singapore’s success down to what he calls the “soft path” approach to their problems.
1:21 · “So the soft path for water is in contrast to what we have done over the last century and more, more than a century, the hard path.
1:29 · To build hard infrastructure, to take more and more water out of nature, to ignore the consequences of our water policies for nature, to build narrow institutions.
1:39 · And the soft path tries to turn that around and say, let’s use water efficiently and carefully.
1:45 · Let’s stop wasting water.
1:47 · Let’s look at new sources of supply.”
1:50 · To understand how Singapore can pull this off, you first need to understand where they’re coming from.


History
1:58 · “The Singapore water story starts with World War 2.”
2:02 · That’s Jon Church, the guy for water at the United Nations.
2:06 · Singaporeans would argue that the story goes back a lot longer, but 1942 is certainly when the issue grabbed the world’s attention.
2:13 · That’s when allied troops, namely British, Australian and Indian forces, were battling fascist Japan on Singapore Island, which at the time was a British colony.
2:24 · The allies depended on imported water which was a bit of a problem when Japanese forces blew up the pipes transporting that water.
2:30 · “The bridge that connects Malaysia and Singapore was bombed.
2:35 · The result was lack of water in the city, a terrible episode of water scarcity.”
2:43 · The Allies lost the battle of Singapore, but after Japan’s overall surrender, the island remained in British hands.
2:50 · It took more than 20 years until it became fully independent.
2:53 · But political liberation didn’t free Singapore from its water crisis: water rationing, catastrophic sanitation, and regular floods continued.
3:01 · With its fate now in its own hands, Singapore began planning for the long-term.
3:06 · Cecilia Tortajada has spent almost three decades researching water policy and innovations around the world and is fascinated by Singapore’s path.
3:15 · “When Singapore became independent, they started planning to be water independent, as well as food independent, energy independent, but to have systems that can sustain stress.
3:28 · That was in 1965 for 2060.”


Step 1: Imported Water
3:32 · Their initial masterplan was fine-tuned over the years into a water strategy which they call their “4 national taps”.
3:40 · First: Water imports Second: Desalination Third: Local Catchment And fourth, something they call “NEWater”.
3:50 · Let’s dive into it!
3:53 · Firstly, Singapore knew there was plenty of water, right here: Two deals to import water from Malaysia in the 60’s, got the taps running again.
4:03 · It’s cheap and millions of liters are pumped over the border every day.
4:07 · But buying half your water from your neighbor isn’t sustainable long-term.
4:12 · On the contrary: From the start, Malaysia made threats to cut off the supply and argued over its price.
4:18 · The tensions have even led to warnings of a military conflict.
4:21 · Singapore’s leaders know their weak spot, so they want to stop importing water by 2061.
4:27 · So, it’s all the more important that the other three taps become more than a drop in the ocean.
4:31 · “Water planning is very important because they have so little water, Singapore must make sure, that this water is used wisely.
4:41 · And the objective of this master plan is to make the most out of every single drop of water.”
4:48 · This means keeping rivers and drains clean, investing billions, starting to collect more water, cleaning it and use what the island state Singapore already has.


Step 2: Desalination
4:57 · For example, this: The ocean!
5:02 · “Desalination, Desalination, Desalination.
5:05 · You take that undrinkable salt water, you remove the salt and you have an unlimited supply of fresh water.”
5:11 · Do you remember?
5:12 · We had an entire video about obtaining fresh water through desalination.
5:16 · It’s used in a number of extremely dry places around the world and is a real gamechanger for some.
5:23 · “Membrane desalination uses pressure.
5:25 · Salt water, here coloured in red for clarity, is pressed through a membrane that is only partially permeable.
5:30 · Fresh water can press through.
5:32 · Here coloured in blue.
5:33 · But the salt is trapped on the other side.”
5:35 · Singapore really pushed to advance this technology.
5:38 · This underground facility for example is state-of-the-art.
5:42 · Normally, it treats used water.
5:44 · In times of drought, it desalinates sea water.
5:47 · On top, people use it as a park.
5:49 · Today, five desalination plants provide up to 25 % of the entire island’s water supply.
5:55 · Singapore plans increase this capacity to meet 30% of its needs in 2060, by which time water use is expected to have doubled.
6:04 · But that’s no way near self-sufficiency.
6:07 · So, what’s next?


Step 3: Local Catchment
6:09 · Bingo! Rain!
6:11 · A lot of it, and Singapore is a master of maxing that out.
6:15 · Two third of the entire state’s surface is used for rainwater catchment.
6:20 · “Basically, the water falls on the roof and then goes through drains and then you make sure that as little water leaks from the drains and is captured by the drainage system and conveyed to reservoirs where it can be stored.
6:43 · And treated for further use.
6:46 · An extensive network of rivers, canals and drains channels the water into 17 reservoirs.
6:51 · The biggest is Marina Barrage, with an area of 10,000 hectares.
6:55 · It holds back fresh water from flowing into the ocean.
6:58 · And helps to control frequent floods.
7:02 · So does this underground tank that catches floodwater in extreme cases when the drains spill over.
7:08 · Even this water could potentially be treated and reused.
7:11 · By 2060, the government wants to use 90% of the land area for rain catchment.


Step 4: NEWater
7:18 · Catching rainwater is one thing, but what about the water already in circulation?
7:25 · “All drainage water is collected, and treated and reused as much as possible.
7:32 · Most countries, they do not invest, not even a fraction of what Singapore is investing.”
7:38 · The water authorities built a 206 kilometer sewage pipe-highway, costing 10 billion dollars that guides the city’s sewage into state-of-the-art reclamation and cleaning facilities.
7:50 · Ok, Singapore is by some measures the 5th richest country in the world so it can afford to splash out like that.
7:56 · It’s also a lot easier to push through such projects when you have the sort of “controlled democracy”, run by the same party, that Singapore has had since independence in 1965.
8:07 · Anyway, the entire city’s underground is basically one big sewer network.
8:12 · But the pride of Singapore’s water strategy is what happens after collecting the water – the treatment.
8:19 · The authorities call it NEWater.
8:21 · It’s produced by microfiltration, reverse osmosis and UV radiation.
8:29 · “Some of that water is so high quality, Singapore is using it in their chip manufacturing industry, which requires ultra-pure water, which is an indication of how good a quality of that water is.”
8:42 · Did you know, that around the world, half of our wastewater is released untreated?
8:46 · And only 11% is actually reused.
8:49 · In Singapore about 30% percent of the entire drinkable and non-drinkable demand can be met by recycling used water.
8:57 · And they want to increase that to 55% by 2060.
9:02 · Most of it is used by industry, only a fraction of it is mixed into the drinking water supply, because we’re all so squeamish.
9:09 · “It’s controversial because we’re taking wastewater which, you know, goes down our drains, we flush it down our toilets, industry dumps wastewater.
9:17 · And we typically think of that as a, a liability, as something to get rid of.”


Policy and Education
9:22 · So how do you get people on board?
9:25 · “Using the flush saver cistern bag and save with every flush!”
9:29 · “Make saving water pay!”
9:30 · “Reduce water consumption!”
9:32 · “Save up to 10 liters of water per hour!”
9:35 · Nationwide campaigns encourage people to install water-saving fittings.
9:38 · And nicely, if you install those fittings, you get discount vouchers for other sustainable products.
9:44 · Digital water meters track each household’s water consumption and detect leaks in pipes.
9:49 · That’s how Singapore comes down to an incredible 5% water loss from leaks.
9:53 · Which is first class.
9:55 · Globally, the average is estimated to be 30%.
9:58 · “What they’ve done incredibly well, in my opinion, is on the side of water education.
10:04 · They’ve educated their community about their water situation, about their water challenges, and about the solutions that they’ve chosen to push.”


Conclusion
10:14 · As good as Singapore is doing, it has big advantages over other countries.
10:18 · Besides being rich and a tightly-controlled society, the city only has a tiny agricultural sector and can focus almost entirely on urban and industrial wastewater.
10:29 · So, they have one problem less as food production pollutes and consumes enormous amounts of fresh water in many parts of the world.
10:36 · Despite that, they’ve shown: a lot is possible.
10:41 · “Everywhere in the world, when we start, again talking about water - when we see our management, how can it be improved?
10:50 · Who would be involved?
10:52 · How can we pay for it?
10:54 · There is always a “but”.
10:55 · “But” can we do it?
10:56 · And in Singapore it’s not.
10:58 · In Singapore it’s: how is it that we are going to do it?
11:01 · So, it’s a very different perspective, its proactive.
11:06 · They move very fast.
11:08 · So once a decision has been taken the things start happening.”
11:14 · So, to sum up: Incentivizing low-cost water-saving fittings could be easy for every government to implement.
11:20 · Desalination is only an option for coastal regions and it requires a lot of energy, often dirty fossil fuels.
11:27 · Singapore’s catchment, treatment and purification facilities are world class, as the result of a lot of investment in innovation and research.
11:34 · “But it turns out that a dollar invested in an efficiency improvement is much more productive than a dollar invested in new supply.”
11:45 · Reusing wastewater seems a no-brainer.
11:47 · It’s safe and tested to work and the tech is available.
11:52 · “This is really important to find the best solutions to every country’s problems, but also long-term planning.
12:01 · Singapore, from all the way from independence has been planning its way through water security.
12:09 · In Singapore it’s extremely high on the political agenda, all the way up to the Prime Minister.
12:16 · It’s something which is mainstreamed in each and every policy adopted and implemented by the country.”
12:25 · Singapore is blazing a trail in tackling some of the world’s biggest water challenges in the face of climate change.
12:30 · It’s not just about money, but also about decision-making, policy and long-term planning.
12:35 · Some of the ingredients with which any region could make it from water rags to riches.

0:02 · Ali: The planet is drying at an unprecedented pace, presenting a critical threat to humanity.
0:07 · That’s according to a new study publish understand in the journal “Science advances.”
0:12 · Researchers found that continental drying is having profound global impact that threaten water availability across the globe.
0:19 · For part of our tipping point coverage, I spoke recently with a climate investigations editor at pro publica, and began by asking him why so much of the Earth is drying out.
0:30 · It’s a mixture of climate change and massive overuse of water resources by people that appears to be drying out a continent, according to a new study out of Arizona state university. And it basically found that rising temperatures are leading to less precipitation in certain places and faster evaporation from both the soil and rivers and surface waters. At the same time that overpumping of ground water aquifers is quickly depleting resources held in those underground reservoirs.
1:02 · Ali: Who’s driving this problem?
1:03 · It’s difficult to parse out the difference between climate change as an effect and the human overpumping of ground water, but those are the two factors. Of course, it’s the I missions from the burning of fossil fuels that is driving the rising temperatures on the planet, and so that is really contributing to a water loss or a water reportioning across the globe.
1:25 · And the ground water pumping is driven by individual use, by farmers, by corporations, by cities around the world. It is becoming the fallback kind of bank account, if you will, of water resources that people in groups are turning to as their surface waters are diminished or as droughts deplete the waters for a shorter period of time. People are looking to those underground reservoirs and pumping more, pumping faster, exploring deeper.
1:51 · Ali: And the study uses nasa satellite images over the course of 20 years to track the evolution of land that’s drying out.
1:59 · Can you walk us through mechanically how that works, how the satellite images were able to capture this change?

2:28 · So now really for the first time these researchers are using that gray satellite data to get a sense of the Earth’s total water supply and then to distinguish between how much of the loss of that water supply is for melting glaciers from climate change, for example, and how much is from something like ground water depletion.

3:19 · They’ve seen that rapid depletion from the very beginning. But it has intensified and accelerated just in the last 10 or 12 years. So that’s particularly alarming. It’s something that led them to write in the paper that this issue is a critical and emerging threat to humanity.

10 Years After Flint, The Fight To Replace Lead Pipes Continues


Duration: 00:13:12

Series: Short Wave

Open Episode in Spotify
Open Series in Spotify
Ten years ago, Flint, Mich. switched water sources to the Flint River. The lack of corrosion control in the pipes caused lead to leach into the water supply of tens of thousands of residents. Pediatrician Mona Hanna-Attisha recognized a public health crisis in the making and gathered data proving the negative health impact on Flint’s young children. In doing so, she and community organizers in Flint sparked a national conversation about lead in the U.S. water system that persists today. Today on the show, host Emily Kwong and science correspondent Pien Huang talk about the state of Flint and other cities with lead pipes. Efforts to replace these pipes hinge on proposed changes to the EPA’s Lead and Copper Rule. Have questions or comments for us to consider for a future episode? You’re listening to SHORT WAVE…

The widespread use of leaded gasoline in the 20th century led to one of the world’s biggest public health and environmental disasters, the effects of which are still present today. Since its development in the 1920s, leaded gasoline has been linked to premature death, cognitive impairment, and behavioral issues in millions around the globe. How was such a toxic substance permitted to be sold, despite the tireless efforts of industrial medicine warriors like Alice Hamilton? In American Poison: A Deadly Invention and the Woman Who Battled for Environmental Justice, award-winning author and historian Daniel Stone tells the story of leaded gasoline - its heroes, its villains, and the lessons we can learn. American cities were once built around people on foot. Downtown streets were packed with shops, apartments, streetcars, theaters, restaurants, and neighborhoods where daily necessities could often be reached without getting into a car. Then, after World War II, America began rebuilding its cities around the automobile.This video explores how highways, suburban expansion, urban renewal, zoning, and massive parking requirements transformed the American landscape. The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 accelerated construction of the Interstate Highway System with the federal government covering 90% of Interstate construction costs. Meanwhile, suburbanization surged: in 1950, 23.3% of Americans lived in suburbs, but by 2000 that figure had reached 50%.Entire urban neighborhoods were demolished or divided by freeways and redevelopment projects, while historic buildings and downtown blocks were increasingly replaced by roads, garages, and surface parking. Parking minimums later reinforced car-oriented development by requiring businesses and housing projects to dedicate substantial amounts of land to automobiles.Discover how America went from compact, walkable neighborhoods to sprawling suburbs and parking lots—and why many cities are now trying to reverse the transformation.ResourcesInterstate System – Federal Highway Administration – FHWA Interstate System History1950 Census Records: A Window to History – U.S. Census Bureau – U.S. Census BureauAmerican Place: The Historic American Buildings Survey at Seventy-Five Years – National Park Service – National Park ServiceUrban Renewal and the Post-War American City – U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development – HUD ArchivesParking Spaces/Community Places – U.S. Environmental Protection Agency – U.S. EPA

Dotted across the Great Basin of the American West are salty, smelly lakes. The largest of these, by far, is the Great Salt Lake in Utah.But a recent report found that water diversions for farming, climate change and population growth could mean the lake essentially disappears within five years. Superfund sites are some of the most polluted areas in the country, containing highly toxic waste such as asbestos, lead, and dioxin. Cleaning them up, which follows a systematic, science-based process as required by law, can take decades.There are more than 1,300 of these sites across the US, from Florida’s Panhandle to the banks of the Rio Grande in New Mexico. They’re found in nearly every state, often near residential areas. The EPA estimates that 78 million people live within three miles of a Superfund site—nearly 1 in 4 Americans.But these waste dumps face a growing threat: the worsening effects of climate change. The EPA has determined that more than 300 Superfund sites are at risk of flooding. The actual number of flood-prone sites, however, may be more than twice that amount, according to a 2021 Government Accountability Office report. Extreme Heat Is the New Normal
New York Times Opinion, 08 28, 2026

Video (15:42)




Description
We filmed “A New Inferno,” the short documentary above, in Phoenix, one of the hottest cities in America, through some of the city’s hottest days of 2025, during one of the hottest years on record globally. On one of our production days, temperatures reached 118 while we were filming outside.
In the face of extreme heat, we documented firefighters and paramedics of the Phoenix Fire Department saving lives in real time. We wanted to call attention to a specialized technique of ice bag immersion for people facing life-threatening heat stroke. We hope that telling their story and showcasing the efficacy of this strategy will encourage wider adoption of this protocol across the country.
Yet this procedure is ultimately a stopgap, as firefighters do their best to adapt to the climate crisis in front of them. The underlying story of heat in Phoenix is one of broader, interlocking crises: homelessness and substance use disorders that are deeply entangled with urban heat, each amplifying the other, illustrating how climate change affects the disenfranchised most brutally.
With our film, we aim to reframe how the public thinks about heat: as an invisible, silent killer reshaping the rhythms of urban life.
Documentary and text by By Nita Blum-Reddick and Jonathan Pickett

How America’s hottest city is trying to cool down

Description
Can trees help save Phoenix from extreme heat?
Subscribe and turn on notifications 🔔 so you don’t miss any videos: http://goo.gl/0bsAjO
It’s time to stop looking at trees as a form of “beautification.” They are, instead, a living form of infrastructure, providing a variety of services that include stormwater management, air filtering, carbon sequestration, and, most importantly for a city like Phoenix, Arizona, they cool the environment around them.
Trees can lower neighborhood temperatures in three ways: 1) Their shade prevents solar radiation from hitting paved surfaces like concrete and asphalt, which absorb energy and rerelease it into the air as heat. 2) Their leaves pull heat from the immediate area in order to evapotranspirate water that’s drawn from the soil. And, 3) If you’re standing under one, a tree protects your body directly from the sun’s rays. If you’ve ever made a summer visit to a dry, hot city like Phoenix, you’ll know how important shade is for making any outdoor experiences tolerable.
As Phoenix deals with a rising frequency of extreme heat waves — which aren’t only deadly, but also cause worrisome spikes in energy demand — the city is looking to trees as part of its heat mitigation strategy. Phoenix isn’t devoid of trees, but they’re distributed unevenly across the city. A quick glance at a satellite image of the metro area reveals substantial green splotches in the north and east and brown ones in the south and west, where many lower-income neighborhoods are located.
So Phoenix recently pledged to reach “tree equity” by 2030, under an agreement with American Forests, a national tree organization. I visited Phoenix recently to take a look at the current state of the city’s urban forest. In this video, we use drone imagery and thermal cameras to understand how the urban design of the city contributes to extreme heat, and what it can do to cool down.

How redlining prevented Black and Brown families from becoming home owners
Harvard Kennedy School, 09 19, 2023

Description
The term “redlining” refers to the practice by banks of excluding Black and Brown Americans from receiving loans to buy homes and make improvements to their communities. Redlining arose during the Great Depression, when the federal government sought to boost homeownership by encouraging banks to lend to more Americans. Many neighborhoods, specifically those with majority Black and Brown residents, were deemed undeserving of these loans. Though redlining was made illegal by the Fair Housing Act, the effects of this practice still reverberate to this day.
In this video, Khalil Gibran Muhammad, Ford Foundation Professor of History, Race, and Public Policy at Harvard Kennedy School and director of the Institutional Antiracism and Accountability Project, provides background on the history and legacy of redlining.

Our mission is to improve public policy and public leadership across the United States and around the world so that people can lead safer, freer, and more prosperous lives. 0:24 · In 1933, in the midst of America’s Great Depression, when unemployment rates were 25% and millions of people were not only out of work, but many of them were houseless, the federal government under President Franklin Delano Roosevelt established an agency called the Home Owners Loan Corporation.

0:01 · The urban environment is a feat of human decision-making— from where to develop street grids lined with large glass office buildings, to which green spaces to preserve for outdoor recreation.


0:13 · How humans make these choices, and the natural environment’s response, can create extremely different ecosystems in neighborhoods just a few blocks away from each other.


0:23 · Researchers delved into dozens of studies to understand what drives these variations.


0:29 · One well documented phenomenon in cities is the relationship between wealth and biodiversity.


0:35 · More affluent areas generally have greater canopy cover, with larger, mature trees, as well as a higher diversity of birds.


0:45 · This is known as the “luxury effect.”


0:48 · Low-income areas typically have more man-made surfaces— including major heat-absorbers like asphalt and concrete, compared to higher-income areas.


0:59 · The lack of shade from trees and vegetation, combined with more asphalt and concrete, makes it hotter in these neighborhoods— a phenomenon known as an “urban heat island.”


1:10 · These communities are also more likely to be near sources of air pollutants, like expansive interstates pumping car exhaust.


1:19 · Although wealth can sometimes predict the outcomes of an urban ecosystem, there isn’t always a clear relationship.


1:26 · In some cases, the racial make-up of a neighborhood is better than income when forecasting canopy cover.


1:33 · Researchers explored studies that highlight how systemic racism shaped our build environment.


1:39 · One glaring example in the United States is residential segregation.


1:44 · From 1933-1968, the federal government limited access to homeownership among Black Americans through a practice known as redlining.


1:55 · Neighborhoods were graded based on the riskiness of providing a mortgage in the area.


2:00 · The grades ranged from A, the most desirable areas, full of wealthy businessmen, to D, neighborhoods considered high-risk investments due to a combination of factors: from their environmental quality and distance from large industrial factories to the main determinant, the presence of foreign-born and Black people.


2:22 · The inability for Black people to buy homes in these neighborhoods meant many types of capital investments left— landlords abandoned their properties, and public services, such as transportation and park maintenance, weren’t prioritized.


2:36 · Today, many U.S. cities still exhibit long-lasting environmental impacts from this discrimination.


2:42 · Neighborhoods which had a “D” grade in the 60s have about half the canopy cover of historically white communities.


2:50 · Some studies evaluate how the current environment relates to historically redlined communities, but researchers did not find any research that traces how ecosystems changed over time because of this segregation.


3:03 · They propose that because habitable regions are more spread out in these areas, animal populations struggle to breed since they are cut off from each other.


3:14 · The reduced breeding options for animals could have decreased gene diversity, an important way for animals to adapt to changing environments.


3:23 · And decreased gene flow of native species could promote the abundance of pest species, like mosquitos and brown rats, which carry diseases that can infect humans.


3:34 · The combination of all these outcomes— from urban heat islands to increased pests— make low-income, marginalized communities far more vulnerable to risks like climate change.


3:47 · Scientists say such evidence shows that conservation and social justice cross paths— especially along neighborhood streets.

0:20 · You’ll find cyclists navigating really narrow strips of space.


0:23 · Americans are used to cars the way that fish are used to water.


0:28 · That’s so ubiquitous in the U.S. that I think for most people, it just never occurred to them that it could be otherwise.


0:35 · But what if there were a way to change that?

0:43 · It turns out Barcelona might have a solution.


0:48 · In 2014, the city was faced with serious air pollution problems.


0:51 · Barcelona and its 35 surrounding municipalities consistently failed to meet the EU’s air quality targets.


0:57 · Studies were showing that air pollution in the region causes 3,500 premature deaths every year.


1:03 · Traffic in the city also causes severe noise pollution.

The Heat Island Effect
0:24 · All of that asphalt, concrete, dark rooftops and tall buildings— they absorb and store heat.
0:31 · And there are a lot of people using a lot of energy— driving cars, riding subways, running the AC.
0:38 · All of these materials and activities either create or retain heat.
0:44 · And all that stored heat causes steeper nighttime highs … when people would otherwise have a chance to cool down.
0:52 · The way all these heat-storing elements are laid out matters quite a bit.
0:57 · In cities laid out in grids, like Phoenix, Chicago, or Washington, D.C., the buildings are closer together, like closely packed coals in a fire, keeping heat in.
1:07 · More space between buildings creates more circulation.
1:11 · Another way to combat this heat island effect is through green space.
1:15 · Parks, trees, plants— they don’t absorb as much heat … they actually send water back in the atmosphere.
1:21 · Between all those hot buildings, that cools things off.
1:25 · Another solution is color.

Paige Bierma, 02-21-2021

Documentary Film (26:48)




Description
In Waking Up to Wildfires, Emmy-winning filmmaker Paige Bierma uses her camera to tell the stories of people most affected by the 2017 North Bay wildfires. We hear from survivors, firefighters, public health officials, community groups and scientists trying to make sense of it all while people struggle to recover and new fires erupt.
The UC Davis Environmental Health Sciences Center produced Waking Up to Wildfires with a grant from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences to help shed light on the plight communities face after these types of disasters.
You’re watching a condensed version (26 minutes long) that’s currently airing on PBS stations across the country. To find out more or get a copy, visit our website at environmentalhealth.ucdavis.edu.

A new approach to fighting malaria



May 31, 2019: A new approach to fighting malaria


Duration: 00:25:28
Released: 2019
Series: Better Off

Open Episode in Spotify
Open Series in Spotify
Each year, more than 200 million people around the world are infected with malaria and more than 400,000 die. For the past two decades, the most successful method of malaria prevention has involved treating bed nets with long-lasting insecticides that kill mosquitoes. But that progress is being threatened as mosquitoes increasingly grow resistant to the most commonly used insecticides. Now, new Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health research offers a potential fresh approach to fighting malaria: directly target the parasite responsible for the disease. A recent study showed that mosquitoes that landed on surfaces coated with the antimalarial compound atovaquone were completely blocked from developing Plasmodium falciparum, the parasite that causes malaria. The study was led by Flaminia Catteruccia, professor of immunology and infectious diseases and Doug Paton , a research fellow at the Harvard Chan School. In this week’s episode we sit down with Paton to discuss the findings—and how they could be used to make progress in the fight against malaria. Full Transcript: hsph.me/malaria-pod

Open Episode in Spotify
Open Series in Spotify
Why do we believe what we believe? Is what we believe the truth? How can we convince others of our beliefs? If you’ve ever found yourself pondering these questions, you know that the answers are rarely clear-cut. We need to form beliefs in order to navigate the world, but how skilled are we at evaluating evidence for those beliefs or weighing new data that contradicts them? In this week’s TPWKY book club episode, Adam Kucharski, Professor at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine joins me to discuss latest book, Proof: The Art and Science of Certainty. With this book, Dr. Kucharski presents a compelling and thoughtful examination of the concept of proof, delving into topics ranging from the justice system (what’s a reasonable doubt?) to infectious disease, clinical design to the founding of this country. And he leaves us with a powerful lesson: what convinced you of something might not convince someone else. Tune in for a fascinating conversation! Hemorrhagic virus? Check. Deadly disease? Check. Mosquito-borne? Check. Affected by animal movement, human activity, and environmental change? Check. Rift Valley Fever has all the markings of a classic TPWKY episode. Transcript
AILSA CHANG, HOST:
It’s CONSIDER THIS, where every day we go deep on one big news story. Today, the devastating flooding in Nepal and its links to climate change. Hundreds are dead, and many more are missing after catastrophic flash flooding along the Tibet-Nepal border.
ANDY THAPA: Nothing is visible - no houses, no roads, no any greenery in those areas and no blue water. Now it’s muddy water now.
CHANG: Andy Thapa is one of the rescuers trying to get to as many survivors as he can. He’s a charter and rescue pilot for a helicopter company in Nepal, and in 20 or so flights over the last two days, he shot some video and shared that video with us.
THAPA: We saw many people stuck in the middle of the mud. Half of the body were inside the mud and they were just seeking for help. But there were no place to land, even no place to drop for the rescue.
CHANG: Thapa said he was able to find survivors in some accessible parts of the mountainous region, but many were in bad shape.
THAPA: Personally, for me, I evacuated more than 120 people. They are muddy, like in their face, in their legs, might be body scratched, hand broken, leg broken and they terrified, you know, unable to speak.
CHANG: He told us about one man who was able to talk with him.
THAPA: He had 10 people in the family, out of which he lost nine in front of his eye.
CHANG: Thapa has been flying the most critically injured people to Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, and the rest to a closer staging area. But there are so many people still stranded. Today, he said he had to leave several hundred people sheltering in a tunnel because the weather just got too bad to fly.
THAPA: But they are very safe and they have enough food to eat. We will just continue with such missions.
CHANG: CONSIDER THIS - climate change is accelerating the frequency of deadly natural disasters. What do we know about the role climate change is playing in the Himalayan region?
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
CHANG: From NPR, I’m Ailsa Chang.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
CHANG: It’s CONSIDER THIS FROM NPR. These deadly flash floods on the border of Nepal and Chinese-administered Tibet are not a surprise to many climate scientists. NPR’s Julia Simon joins us now to explain why. Hi, Julia.
JULIA SIMON, BYLINE: Hello, Ailsa.
CHANG: So the way I understand it, this flooding - it came from a glacier - right? - that collapsed. Is that correct?
SIMON: Yeah. So the reports are still preliminary, but many scientists think this was a glacier collapsing - this giant chunk of ice that snapped off, triggering the floods. This mass of ice and rock and mud and water - it started ripping down this Himalayan river valley, down through these villages, destroying communities. If you’ve seen the videos, you can see it’s this avalanche of deadly debris.
CHANG: Yeah. And I mean, these glaciers, they’ve been around for thousands of years, right? So…
SIMON: Right.
CHANG: …To have a chunk of glacier just snap off now seems like a huge deal.
SIMON: It does. But sadly, many scientists are not so surprised that this could happen, Ailsa, and that’s because of human-caused climate change. These glaciers that were once stable - they’re disappearing. NPR has been reporting on Nepal’s glaciers for years. A team from NPR traveled to Nepal in 2022. They were climbing up a moraine. That’s a massive pile of boulders created by a glacier. But when NPR’s Rebecca Hersher got to the top, there was no glacier in sight.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)
REBECCA HERSHER: Oh, wow.
(SOUNDBITE OF WATER SPLASHING)
SIMON: That’s the sound of water. There was only water - this huge lake - where a glacier should have been, Ailsa. The glacier had melted, and glacial lake floods are a growing threat. In recent years, multiple glacial lake floods have displaced and killed people. Scientists warn that an estimated 15 million people around the world are at risk from such floods.
CHANG: Wow. So just how unstable are these melting glaciers?
SIMON: Yeah. So NPR spoke with Alton Byers about this. He’s at the Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research at the University of Colorado at Boulder. He says he’s surprised how fast the permafrost - that’s the continuously frozen ice, soil and rock that’s held the mountains together for millennia - it’s now changing.
ALTON BYERS: The analogy I and my colleagues use is take a stick of butter out of the refrigerator and put it on the counter. It’s going to get softer and it’s going to lose its structural integrity.
SIMON: Yeah. So these melting glaciers - they pose deadly risks to the communities in their path.
CHANG: I mean, we’re seeing it right now. So…
SIMON: Yeah.
CHANG: …What are some solutions here to prevent the kind of disaster that we are seeing in Nepal, for example, a disaster that is caused by melting glaciers?
SIMON: Well, the first thing is better alert systems. It seems right now, like, Nepal’s flood warning system wasn’t equipped to handle this, despite quite a bit of investment in those warning systems over the last decade or so. And it’s important to mention this area has seen flash floods before. But we also know the primary driver of global warming is the burning of fossil fuels, like oil, gas and coal. The solutions to transition away from fossil fuels are out there, Ailsa. They are scalable. They’re affordable. They’re reliable. They include solar energy, wind energy and batteries.
CHANG: That is NPR climate and energy correspondent Julia Simon. Thank you, Julia.
SIMON: Thank you, Ailsa.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
CHANG: It’s CONSIDER THIS FROM NPR. I’m Ailsa Chang.

In August 2005, one of the most powerful storms ever recorded in the Gulf of Mexico barrelled toward the United States. When Hurricane Katrina finally struck land, it devastated hundreds of miles of shoreline, but the disaster that captured the world’s attention unfolded in one place above all: the city of New Orleans.   Within hours of the storm passing, the flood defence levees meant to protect the city broke, and it began to fill with water. What followed the natural disaster was a crisis that raised profound questions about preparedness, inequality, and the ability and willingness of a modern nation to protect one of its own great cities.   But why was New Orleans so vulnerable in the first place? What was the response in the wake of the hurricane and flooding? And what did the disaster reveal about the systems of engineering, government and society that were supposed to protect it? This is a Short History Of Hurricane Katrina. A Noiser podcast production. Hosted by John Hopkins. Superfund sites are some of the most polluted areas in the country, containing highly toxic waste such as asbestos, lead, and dioxin. Cleaning them up, which follows a systematic, science-based process as required by law, can take decades.There are more than 1,300 of these sites across the US, from Florida’s Panhandle to the banks of the Rio Grande in New Mexico. They’re found in nearly every state, often near residential areas. The EPA estimates that 78 million people live within three miles of a Superfund site—nearly 1 in 4 Americans.But these waste dumps face a growing threat: the worsening effects of climate change. The EPA has determined that more than 300 Superfund sites are at risk of flooding. The actual number of flood-prone sites, however, may be more than twice that amount, according to a 2021 Government Accountability Office report. Floodwaters can move toxic waste into neighboring communities, which threatens drinking water, agriculture, and broader ecosystem health.Read more at sciencefriday.comTranscripts for each segment will be available after the show airs on sciencefriday.com. The climate crisis isn’t a distant threat — it’s already here, and it’s deadly. But keeping people cool is surprisingly complicated.

Science journalist Miles O’Brien puts himself in the hot seat — literally — to find out what it feels like when the body’s cooling system starts to fail.

The climate crisis isn’t a distant threat — it’s already here, and it’s deadly. But keeping people cool is surprisingly complicated.
In Sydney, Australia, physiologist Ollie Jay is tackling the problem by studying how the human body responds to extreme heat. The ultimate goal is to create low-cost cooling strategies for people without access to air conditioning — those most at risk from extreme heat. Science journalist Miles O’Brien puts himself in the hot seat — literally — to find out what it feels like when the body’s cooling system starts to fail.

Resolve to Solve with Miles O’Brien
Miles O’Brien travels the globe searching for solutions to climate, water, and health crises. From building sea curtains in Antarctica to restoring wildlife in Argentina, the answers are closer than we think thanks to people with a “Resolve to Solve.”

0:01 · MILES O’BRIEN: At the iconic Sydney Opera House, I met a scientist looking for an answer.
0:06 · Ollie Jay runs the Heat and Health Research Center at the University of Sydney.
0:13 · Lay the context for us a little bit on Australia, its climate, and the heat impacts you deal with here.
0:21 · We have an increased prevalence of heat waves.
0:23 · They’re greater intensity, the maximum temperature records are being beaten regularly.
0:28 · Among, uh, high income countries, we’re actually the most susceptible to the impacts of extreme heat on human health and well-being.
0:35 · For a researcher such as yourself, trying to find solutions, ways to adapt, this is the perfect laboratory, isn’t it?
0:41 · JAY: Absolutely.
0:42 · We take time to understand the nature of the problem before we start trying to develop solutions, because we don’t want to go down that route that a lot of academics do of finding solutions to problems that don’t exist.
0:52 · O’BRIEN: Ollie and his team are looking for smarter, more efficient ways to keep people safe and cool as the global thermostat rises.
1:01 · ♪ ♪ That was on his mind when I met him on a steamy Saturday at the University of Sydney Cricket Club Oval.
1:11 · (bat cracks) A match like this can last two long days, six to eight hours each.
1:19 · That was big!
1:20 · (cheers and applause) On the sidelines, Ollie Jay and his team were setting up a curious contraption they call the EMU.
1:30 · It’s a flightless Australian bird, but also something called the Environmental Measurement Unit.
1:35 · O’BRIEN: Mm-hmm.
1:36 · Like MaRTy in Phoenix, EMU measures four key parameters: air temperature, humidity, radiant temperature and wind speed.
1:47 · We measure temperature in this device right here.
1:50 · We can move air in a certain way across that temperature sensor to get a very accurate read on what the temperature of the air is in the shade.
1:57 · O’BRIEN: Humidity is measured in that same white chamber.
2:01 · Above it is a copper sphere that is painted matte black.
2:07 · It measures radiation that comes directly from the sun and bounces off the various surfaces surrounding an athlete.
2:15 · JAY: And then using all of this information, we can model how hot someone’s going to get, and therefore what their rate of dehydration might be.
2:21 · And, you know, potentially how much water they need to drink in order to maintain hydration.
2:29 · O’BRIEN: A short walk away from the cricket oval is Ollie’s lab.
2:33 · And that’s where he’s built another novel tool to better understand how heat affects the human body.
2:39 · It’s a climate chamber.
2:42 · Think of it as a science oven, and I’m on the menu.
2:47 · JAY: Just be careful of the step there.
2:49 · Here we go, Miles.
2:50 · O’BRIEN: You’re not messing around.
2:52 · JAY: No, we’re not messing around. O’BRIEN: All right.
2:54 · Reporting for scientific duty.
2:55 · I was finally going to find out what it’s like to be an order of French fries, waiting under the heat lamp on a short-order shelf.
3:05 · Before I got this far, I swallowed a horse pill.
3:08 · Right down the gullet there.
3:10 · A thermometer with a tiny transmitter inside that tracked my core temperature.
3:15 · I’m hot stuff.
3:16 · They took my blood pressure.
3:18 · Applied a strap to track my heart rate and a mask that measured the amount of oxygen I was consuming, to help estimate how much heat my body was generating on its own.
3:30 · JAMES SMALLCOMBE: If you can just blow out for me.
3:31 · (blows) Yep, that’s tight enough, that’s perfect.
3:34 · Your cardiovascular system seems to be in pretty good nick, uh, Miles, we’ve got, you know, great blood pressure and your resting heart rate’s nice and, uh, nice and low, so.
3:43 · Objective evidence demonstrating your very good health.
3:46 · O’BRIEN: He put it to the test by simulating one of the worst weather disasters in modern U.S. history: the heat wave in Chicago in 1995.
3:57 · More than 700 people died.
3:59 · Researchers concluded a working air conditioner would have prevented half the fatalities.
4:05 · And living alone doubled the risk of death.
4:07 · It became a stark lesson in how vulnerability and isolation can turn extreme heat into a mass-casualty disaster.
4:17 · Almost for the first time, it placed extreme heat on the radar of public health officials and actually seeing that it is responsible for excess death and morbidity.
4:27 · O’BRIEN: The tragedy exposed something deeper than weather.
4:31 · It was about inequality, and neglect.
4:35 · That summer, Chicago made it painfully clear heat doesn’t strike evenly, and it kills quietly.
4:44 · We’re doing this from the perspective of trying to understand the settings that the most vulnerable are going to be in, and then developing solutions that are fit for purpose in those settings.
4:54 · O’BRIEN: Here in the chamber, the temperature was 104 degrees Fahrenheit, with humidity between 50% and 60%.
5:03 · It was pretty miserable.
5:06 · I feel like a cheeseburger just off the grill.
5:08 · The human body cools itself by sweating, but that only works if the sweat can evaporate.
5:14 · At this temperature and humidity, it can’t.
5:19 · The air is nearly saturated.
5:21 · The sweat just sits there, and the body keeps heating up.
5:27 · It’s a huge challenge for human survival.
5:30 · What we know is that the people who are most vulnerable won’t have access to air conditioning.
5:34 · They most likely won’t have access to things like cooling shelters as well.
5:38 · They’ll be sheltering at home in place.
5:40 · So the question is, what type of activities, what type of risk reduction cooling strategies can these people use that is most effective at blunting that physiological heat strain that generates inside the body that we know is harmful to human health?
5:53 · O’BRIEN: He’s exploring cooling strategies for people who can’t afford to live in air-conditioned comfort.
6:00 · Practical, low-cost ways to survive the heat.
6:04 · Things like immersing your feet in water so they act like radiators.
6:09 · And using fans which, under the right conditions, can significantly reduce the effects of heat stress.
6:16 · These are the kinds of things that can help the most vulnerable among us, during a heat wave like Chicago in 1995.
6:26 · With the proper prior planning on that, could those deaths have been preventable?
6:31 · Most of them?
6:32 · There’s a, there’s a saying, um, in the heat health space that every heat-related death is preventable.
6:40 · O’BRIEN: Globally, heat kills about a half-a-million people every year.
6:45 · And in the U.S., the fatalities are growing at an alarming rate.
6:50 · In 2023, more than 2,300 died from heat in the U.S.
6:55 · About three times more than a decade ago.
6:58 · Far greater than the average toll for hurricanes and wildfires.
7:03 · They grab the headlines, but heat has always been the most lethal consequence of climate change, by far.
7:11 · Outside this window in Sydney, intense heat is everywhere– quiet, invisible and relentless.
7:20 · Ah.
7:22 · (sighs) Sheesh.
7:23 · After I’d mopped myself up, Ollie and I went from the frying pan to the fire.
7:31 · He took me on a walking tour of the University of Sydney campus.
7:35 · Born and raised in Wales, with a stop in Canada along the way, Ollie actually earned his PhD studying cold temperatures.
7:45 · But in 2014, Sydney beckoned.
7:48 · Suddenly, he was on the opposite end of the earth and the thermometer.
7:53 · Australia being a hot place, and it is a hot place, I figure that if, Australian-based researchers, if we can’t get a handle on these problems, and we can’t find a solution, then there’s very little chance that anyone else will.
8:06 · O’BRIEN: Plenty of scientists study the climate and the relentless rise of temperatures.
8:10 · But far fewer connect the dots to the impact on human health.
8:15 · How heat affects real bodies, in real time, in a warming world.
8:20 · It’s a mistake to overlook human physiology as you try to come up with some answers here, right?
8:25 · If you think about it from a health perspective, obviously, the hot weather is a problem.
8:29 · But the real problem is the hot person in the hot environment.
8:32 · ♪ ♪ O’BRIEN: It was time for us to solve that problem.
8:36 · We met up with his partner Allison and their adorable, precocious daughter Lottie.
8:41 · ALLISON: Ready to go to the beach?
8:43 · O’BRIEN: They took me to Coogee Beach, a short walk from their home in Sydney.
8:49 · Becoming a parent has changed the way he thinks about his work.
8:54 · It’s sharpened his focus and redoubled his resolve to solve.
9:00 · There are lots of solutions, but I think what we’ve got to do is focus on not just climate change mitigation, ensuring that the choices that we make don’t aggravate the problem in the future, but also got to face that we’ve got to adapt to a warmer world.
9:13 · We need to do both of them at the same time.
9:15 · It would be bad if all of that back and forth led to inertia and apathy. JAY: Well, it’s exactly right.
9:21 · People need to have hope in order to act.
9:22 · Otherwise, we just bury our head in the sand and try to pretend it’s not happening when it is.
9:26 · O’BRIEN: In the sand. JAY: Here we are.
9:28 · O’BRIEN: I see what you’re doing there, man.
9:30 · Nicely done, nicely done. (Ollie laughing) ♪ ♪

This is one a. I’m Naila Budu in for Jen White. Extreme heat isn’t just an inconvenience. It’s a growing public health threat. Climate change is making heat waves hotter and more frequent, and high temps aren’t just being reported in the daytime. Nighttime temperatures are higher than ever.
